transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Karen (Seabright Head of Platform), Marcus (Seabright ML), Sofia (Seabright Security), Diego (Product)

Summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated capacity — reserved GPUs, isolation/networking, burst strategy, and scaling expectations. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC). Main concerns: predictable latency, data isolation, SOC2 + KMS, and cost predictability under heavy batch workloads.

Topics: dedicated capacity, autoscaling, burst, reserved GPU pools, data residency, encryption/KMS, SOC2/SSO, benchmarking plan, next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex Morgan from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya and Daniel from our se- --- solutions engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Karen: Good, thanks. We got a few folks on our side, I'm Karen Ito, head of platform at Seabright. Marcus is our ML lead, Sofia handles security, Diego is product.
[00:12] Alex: Awesome. The goal for today is to understand your deployment needs — whether Dedicated reserved GPU capacity makes sense, isolation and networking requirements, and how you want burst / scaling to work. We'll also capture any security asks.
[00:20] Marcus: Yeah, high level we're trying to decide between Redwood's hosted API for fast iteration, or moving to Dedicated when we hit production scale. Our main workloads are real-time chat assistants and nightly batch embeddings for search. Latency is critical for chat, embeddings are more throughput-y.
[00:35] Priya: Helpful — do you have ballpark qps and p50/p95 latency targets for the chat flows? Also what models are you evaluating?
[00:42] Marcus: For chat, we're looking at around 200 qps peak per region, p50 below 80ms if possible, p95 below 250ms. Our current prototype uses a 20B model quantized to int8, running on A100-ish hardware. For embeddings we push large nightly batches — think millions of rows spread across a 6 hour window.
[01:05] Alex: Great. So Dedicated could give you reserved GPU pools to hit predictable throughput and lower variance on latency. Important to know: are you ok with pooling across teams, or do you need strict single-tenant isolation?
[01:16] Karen: For regulatory reasons, we need logical isolation and audit trail. Physical single-tenant isn't required yet, but strict tenancy boundaries, RBAC, and audit logs are non-negotiable. Also we use a customer-managed KMS.
[01:30] Sofia: To expand — keys must be in our AWS KMS and Redwood needs to support envelope encryption and not retain plaintext tokens. We also want full request/response audit logs stored in our S3 for 7 years.
[01:44] Priya: Notes — we support integrations with customer KMS/HSM and can configure audit log exports. For long-term retention we recommend pushing logs to your S3; we can provide the export pipeline. A couple of details there may be different depending on Dedicated vs Private deployment.
[01:58] Diego: Can you clarify the difference between Dedicated and Private. We saw the docs but it was a bit fuzzy for the infra team.
[02:06] Alex: Sure. Hosted is our managed multi-tenant API. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools in our infra with logical isolation, VPC peering options, and per-tenant capacity guarantees — good compromise for enterprise customers who need predictability but not full on-prem. Private is the customer-managed control plane — VPC or on-prem package for full control and air-gapped requirements. Dedicated sits in the middle: we still manage the infra, but capacity is reserved and networking can be configured to meet compliance.
[02:30] Marcus: For our use case, Dedicated sounds right if it meets the KMS and audit requirements. Also curious about burst — we have spiky traffic from marketing pushes, could we burst beyond our reserved GPUs temporarily?
[02:44] Priya: Yes, we support burst capacity. There are two models — queued burst via autoscaling of ephemeral GPUs and a fallback to compatible cheaper models. You can configure policy: e.g., allow up to 2x reserved for short windows, or fall back to a quantized variant that trades some quality for capacity. Burst configuration is part of the Dedicated offering and can be tuned per route.
[03:03] Karen: Important: during burst we cannot send any PII to a shared pool without encryption and audit trail. Is the KV cache stored in Redwood or in-managed per-customer store? I've seen mention of KV cache and prefix caching in the docs.
[03:17] Daniel: The KV cache (our 'KV cache') is sharded per-customer on Dedicated; prefix/KV caching reduces per-token compute for repeated prompts. When bursting to shared capacity, we either bring a compatible variant into your reserved pool or use a logically isolated ephemeral buffer — but we will honor encryption and never write plaintext outside your configured storage. There are some implementation details we can share in a security doc.
[03:37] Sofia: We'll need that security doc. Also, how does network egress work with VPC peering? We need CIDR ranges and flow logs for our firewall team.
[03:46] Priya: We can provide peering IP blocks and flow log integration. For Dedicated we set up a private peering link or PrivateLink depending on region. Flow logs can be pushed to your CloudWatch/S3. We'll include the network diagram in the follow-up.
[04:00] Marcus: Back to performance — you mentioned kernel selection and quantization profiles that Redwood uses. With our 20B int8 setup we saw decent perf on A100, but we want to understand the expected tokens/sec per GPU for our prompt mix. Can Redwood run a benchmark with our sample payloads?
[04:18] Alex: Yes, we typically run a benchmark. We'll need your sample payloads and ideal SLOs. For Dedicated we can spin up a benchmark cluster matched to your reserved config; we'll measure p50/p95 and throughput. We'll also provide model recommendations — sometimes smaller quantized models with optimized kernels beat a larger model for cost/perf.
[04:35] Diego: Cost — how is billing handled for dedicated? Do we pay fixed monthly for reserved and then overage for burst? Also curious about unit economics for embeddings batch jobs.
[04:46] Alex: Dedicated is typically committed capacity — monthly or annual reserved GPU pools at a discounted rate. Burst/overage is charged at a predefined rate for ephemeral capacity used above reservation. For embeddings we can provide TCO scenarios: reserved capacity sized for steady-state plus burst for peaks, or schedule spot-style batch windows to use spare capacity. We'll send a TCO sheet with examples.
[05:04] Karen: For procurement we'll need an estimate for annual committed plus an example invoice breakdown. Also our legal team will want the security addendum and SOC 2 report.
[05:13] Alex: Absolutely — next steps we'll send pricing, SOC2, and the network/security docs.
[05:18] Sofia: For SOC2 we might need more details on change management and patching cadence for Dedicated nodes. Do you manage kernel and driver updates or is that controlled by Redwood with a notice window?
[05:29] Priya: Redwood manages node maintenance; we have a scheduled maintenance window and provide notices. For Dedicated we can offer a maintenance SLA and coordinate maintenance outside your peak windows where possible. We also have options for conservative patching policies on committed clusters.
[05:44] Marcus: A couple more technical questions — 1) what GPU families do you support for Dedicated (A100, H100?), 2) is autoscaling per-route or per-pool, and 3) how fast is cold-start for an idle model?
[05:57] Daniel: We support A100 and H100 clusters depending on region; H100 gives better large-model perf for attention kernels. Autoscaling is policy-driven and can be configured per-route and per-pool; that lets you reserve for chat routes and separate pools for batch embeddings. Cold-start depends on model size and quantization — for cached KV state and compiled kernels we typically see warm-up in 5-30s for larger models; we also support pre-warming where predictable.
[06:20] Marcus: That warm-up is acceptable if we pre-warm before a campaign. But for live chat we need p95 under 250ms — so reserved pool is required.
[06:28] Alex: Makes sense. We'll size the reserved pool to keep chat SLOs. One design pattern is to reserve capacity for steady-state chat load and use burst for surges. For embeddings, schedule batch windows or use dedicated batch pool with lower-cost GPUs.
[06:41] Diego: Any complexities with data residency? We have customers in EU and want embeddings stored in eu-central. Does Dedicated support region pinning?
[06:50] Priya: Yes, you can pin pools to regions. For data-at-rest residency we can ensure embeddings and logs are stored in your chosen region and exported to your bucket. Some features like global failover require replication — we'll call that out in the doc.
[07:04] Karen: Ok — two governance items: 1) RBAC and least-privilege access for developer teams, and 2) how rollouts/rollback work for model updates (we do canaries internally).
[07:15] Alex: We have RBAC and SSO/SAML integrations. For rollouts we support canary deployments, A/B testing, and automatic fallback policies. You can pin routes to a model version and gradually roll traffic. We'll share an ops runbook.
[07:28] Sofia: Also need assurance that logs and request data used for model improvements are opt-in and data is not used by default for training.
[07:36] Alex: Absolutely, by default customer data isn't used to train models. We'll document data handling controls in the security pack.
[07:42] Marcus: For the benchmark, who will own the infra for test runs? Do we give Redwood temporary creds into our VPC or do you run tests in your environment with sample payloads?
[07:53] Priya: We can do both. Many customers prefer Redwood to run an initial benchmark in our infra with representative payloads, then a joint run in customer's environment via a peered test account if you want end-to-end numbers including VPC networking. We'll coordinate with your infra team.
[08:09] Karen: We'll prefer a joint run for final sign-off.
[08:12] Diego: Timeline — we're aiming for an internal launch in Q2. What is typical lead time to provision a Dedicated pool?
[08:20] Alex: Provisioning depends on GPU availability and region, but typically 2–6 weeks for a Dedicated pool. If you need faster, we can explore a hybrid approach: start on hosted with reserved capacity commitments and migrate to Dedicated as capacity is provisioned.
[08:34] Marcus: Cost and procurement cycles aside, that's reasonable. Procurement will want pricing and terms for 12-month commit.
[08:40] Alex: We'll include 12-month and monthly examples in the TCO.
[08:44] Sofia: Last security note — we need to review service penetration testing posture and SOC 2 Type II. Also vulnerability disclosure program details.
[08:52] Alex: We'll include pen test summary and vulnerability program info in the security pack.
[08:56] Karen: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[08:59] Alex: Recap: Redwood to send Dedicated pricing and TCO, SOC2 and security docs, network peering diagram, autoscaling/burst config examples, and coordinate benchmark dates. Seabright to send sample payloads and list of infra stakeholders.
[09:13] Marcus: I'll put together sample payloads and expected SLO table.
[09:17] Sofia: I'll compile the compliance questions and send to Alex + Priya.
[09:20] Alex: Perfect. We'll target the week of Mar 15 for the joint benchmark. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD with the docs.
[09:29] Karen: Thanks all.
[09:31] [call ends]
